title: I built a browser incremental game almost entirely with AI — validation became the real development work
author: Fearless-Chart7704
selftext:
I recently released Emoji Alchemy, a free browser incremental game where players combine emojis, discover elements, build production facilities, and compete on a live ranking.

The project was built almost entirely through AI-assisted development. AI generated and refactored most of the code, helped produce the visual assets and UI, and drafted localization. My role was to direct the design, review the output, test the actual game, identify failures, and keep iterating until it could be deployed.

The surprising part was that generating features was much easier than proving that they worked together. The most useful checks ended up being:

• validating that all 150 elements and 145 recipes are reachable
• checking the production-facility dependency graph for circular or impossible unlocks
• testing mobile layouts and text overflow across 16 languages
• keeping ranking and progression validation on the server instead of trusting client saves
• separating plausible-looking AI output from behavior that survives a complete playthrough

The main lesson for me is that AI can produce a large first pass very quickly, but automated validation and repeated hands-on testing become a major part of the development process. A system can look complete while still containing one unreachable recipe or a progression dependency that blocks the late game.

You can play it here: [https://smilejsu82.itch.io/emoji-alchemy](https://smilejsu82.itch.io/emoji-alchemy)

For people shipping AI-assisted games: which validation or testing method has caught the most subtle failures in your projects? I would also appreciate observations about the first ten minutes of progression.

comments.body:
that's pretty cool. I've experimented with emojis

microsoft has open sourced them with 3 diff types which is cool if you wanna let players customize how their emojis look. I took it even one step further, they have black emoji outlines, but I had a script that converted them all to white, and then you could use a color picker to pick whatever color you wanted since any color blends with white

[https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-emoji](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-emoji)

and if you wanna have some animations they have the animated emojis as well  
[https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-emoji-animated](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-emoji-animated)

it's totally free to use in your projects, your agent could easily do this to your game. Just a thought that might be cool. I played this game called merge maestro that used these emojis and got me on a kick making games with emojis as the art
